messages.message:
How the parameterized response is built:

  • Full MC characterization - Monte Carlo over the full energy×angle(×distance) grid of the selected profile. Most accurate, especially near the detector and off-axis; most run time.
  • Quick MC (transfer) - Monte Carlo only along the on-axis energy backbone (plus, optionally, a few source-angle anchors); the exact ray-traced geometry then carries the response to other distances and angles (EFFTRAN-style efficiency transfer). Roughly a tenth of the Monte Carlo - typically around a minute. On-axis accuracy is about 1% beyond a few detector-widths; queries near contact or far off-axis are flagged and carry an honestly inflated uncertainty.
  • From measured curve - no Monte Carlo at all: the DRF's own measured efficiency points (or its fitted curve) are anchored at their measurement distance and transferred to other distances/angles through the ray-traced geometry. Instant and deterministic - it rebuilds automatically as you edit the geometry. The classic lab efficiency-transfer workflow, made 3-D and Rayleigh-aware.
This DRF currently uses a quick transfer response; run a Full MC characterization for the best near-field / off-axis accuracy.

Controls how close to the detector the response stays accurate - i.e. how much extra Monte Carlo is spent characterizing the near-field. All three profiles cover the full front hemisphere (source angle 0° on-axis through 90° grazing) and the detector's whole energy range; they differ only in the closest distance they model. (Sources behind the detector face - angles > 90°, e.g. Marinelli beakers - are not modeled by any profile.)

  • Far-field only - no near-field model at all. Accurate from roughly a few detector-widths outward; queries closer than that are flagged (not silently corrected). Cheapest. Use for fixed, large-standoff installations or search detectors.
  • General (default) - adds a near-field model down to about one detector transverse size (a few cm). Covers typical lab bench and hand-held measurements. Moderate extra cost.
  • Extra near detail - scans the near-field denser and all the way down to contact (about half a detector size, ~0.5 cm), with fine angular coverage close-in. Use for contact, well, or swipe counting, or anything held right against the endcap. Most Monte Carlo, but the only profile accurate at contact off-axis.

The per-node Monte-Carlo statistical target: how tightly each point of the response is computed. Tighter means less statistical noise baked into the stored response, at more run time (cost scales roughly as 1 / precision² - halving the target is about 4× the work).

  • Fast (1%) - a quick preview, or small/high-efficiency detectors.
  • Normal (0.3%) - a good balance for most detectors (default).
  • Balanced (relaxed high-E) - keeps low-energy points tight but relaxes the expensive high-energy points, for about a 2× faster run at nearly the same accuracy.
  • Thorough (0.1%) - a high-quality reference; noticeably slower.
  • Custom - enter your own per-node target (e.g. 0.2%).

This is the statistical precision only; the response's overall accuracy also depends on how finely the energy/angle/distance grids are placed, so tightening precision helps but has diminishing returns.

How many source angles the quick Monte Carlo anchors the transfer at.

  • On-axis only - the geometry kernel alone carries the angular dependence. Off-axis full-energy-peak efficiencies are good to roughly 3-4%, and for HPGe the total efficiency (used by cascade-summing corrections) can drift off-axis. Fine for on-axis measurements.
  • 3 angles - a few extra MC anchors versus on-axis only; brings off-axis full-energy-peak accuracy under about 1% and tabulates a real angular total-efficiency shape (recommended, especially for HPGe).

The source-to-detector distance the efficiency curve is valid at - the anchor the transfer holds fixed. Pre-filled from where the curve is pinned to data: its stated measurement distance when it has one, otherwise a comfortably far-field distance. When the DRF carries raw measured points at a single distance, the points pin it and it cannot be edited.

Distances are measured from the detector face (or the geometry's selected reference point).

Source-to-detector distance for the absolute efficiency curves (per emitted gamma). Each curve is the full-energy-peak efficiency versus energy at a source angle of 0°, 22.5°, 45°, 62.5° and 90° from the detector axis; the dashed line is the angle-flat far-field (infinite-plane) reference. The shaded band around each curve is its 1-sigma uncertainty, and a curve whose legend is annotated (e.g. "near-field unmodeled") is outside the response's validated regime at this distance. Intrinsic efficiency (per gamma striking the face) is distance-independent in the far field.
